Standard Library > bytes: Byte Sequences (sla_std)

bytes.sla: Byte Sequences (sla_std)

A pure-SLA byte-sequence type in sla_std (source sla_std/bytes.sla in sa_plugin_sla, mirrored byte-identically into layola13/sla). It gives SLA programs the CPython bytes semantics at the SLA level: an immutable-by-convention sequence of byte values 0–255, with slicing, search, comparison, hex / base64 conversion and a CPython-shaped repr. The type itself is one struct:

struct Bytes {
    data: Vec<u8>,
}

Value semantics. SLA has no &mut, so every “mutating” operation takes &Bytes and returns a fresh Bytes; the argument is never modified. The single exception is the psa-carrier primitive __psa_bytes_set_h (see below), which exists for the psa runtime and is not part of the general surface.

There is deliberately no bytes_to_str. SLA has a String.as_bytes() but no String-from-bytes constructor, so conversions that would produce text in CPython (hex(), base64 encoding, repr()) return a Bytes holding the ASCII payload instead. Bridging a Bytes to a string value is the psa glue layer's job, not this module's.

Import

@import "sla_std/bytes.sla"

Function Table (from sla_std/bytes.sla)

SignatureDescription
bytes_new() -> BytesAn empty Bytes
bytes_clone(b: &Bytes) -> BytesAn independent copy
bytes_from_vec(v: &Vec<u8>) -> BytesCopy a byte vector into a Bytes
bytes_from_str(s: &String) -> BytesThe raw UTF-8 bytes of the string, copied (the CPython bytes(s, "utf-8") case; no encoding argument exists at this layer)
bytes_len(b: &Bytes) -> i64Number of bytes
bytes_get(b: &Bytes, idx: i64) -> u8Byte at idx; negative indices count from the end; out of range panics 9010
bytes_set(b: &Bytes, idx: i64, x: u8) -> BytesA copy with byte idx replaced (negative indices allowed); out of range panics 9010
bytes_push(b: &Bytes, x: u8) -> BytesA copy with x appended
bytes_concat(a: &Bytes, b: &Bytes) -> BytesConcatenation
bytes_repeat(a: &Bytes, n: i64) -> Bytesa repeated n times; n <= 0 gives an empty Bytes
bytes_slice(b: &Bytes, lo: i64, hi: i64, step: i64) -> BytesCPython slice.indices semantics: negative bounds count from the end and are clamped; step == 0 panics 9013
bytes_eq(a: &Bytes, b: &Bytes) -> boolByte-wise equality
bytes_cmp(a: &Bytes, b: &Bytes) -> i64Byte-wise lexicographic order, normalized to -1 / 0 / 1; a shorter prefix sorts first
bytes_find(hay: &Bytes, needle: &Bytes) -> i64Index of the first occurrence, or -1; an empty needle matches at 0 (CPython)
bytes_contains(hay: &Bytes, needle: &Bytes) -> boolbytes_find(...) != -1
bytes_to_hex(b: &Bytes) -> BytesLowercase hex, no separators (CPython bytes.hex()), as an ASCII-payload Bytes
bytes_from_hex(s: &String) -> BytesCPython bytes.fromhex: ASCII whitespace is skipped only between byte pairs — a space inside a pair, an odd digit count, or a non-hex digit panics 9011
bytes_to_b64(b: &Bytes) -> BytesStandard base64 with = padding and no line breaks; callers that need wrapped output (e.g. plistlib <data>) chunk it themselves
bytes_from_b64(s: &String) -> BytesStrict base64: whitespace is skipped, every other character must be in the alphabet or trailing = padding, and the cleaned length must be a multiple of 4; anything else panics 9012 (CPython's lenient ignore-junk mode is deliberately not taken)
bytes_repr(b: &Bytes) -> BytesCPython repr: b prefix, single quotes unless the payload has a single quote and no double quote; backslash / the quote char / \t \n \r are escaped, every other non-printable byte becomes \xNN
__psa_bytes_set_h(p: ptr, i: i64, x: u8)psa runtime primitive (substrate gap #22): in-place write of one byte through a Box<Bytes> carrier pointer. Not a general-purpose API; bounds failures trap on the SLA runtime's own index check

Example 1: Build, Concatenate, Search (a runnable program)

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sla_std/bytes.sla"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let s1 = format("hello");
    let b = bytes_from_str(&s1);
    let s2 = format(" world");
    let w = bytes_from_str(&s2);
    let c = bytes_concat(&b, &w);
    let s3 = format("world");
    let ndl = bytes_from_str(&s3);
    println("len={}", bytes_len(&c));
    println("first={}", (bytes_get(&c, 0) as i64));
    println("last={}", (bytes_get(&c, -1) as i64));
    println("cmp={}", bytes_cmp(&b, &c));
    println("find={}", bytes_find(&c, &ndl));
    return 0;
}

Output (verified):

len=11
first=104
last=100
cmp=-1
find=6

Only numeric facts are printed: with no Bytes→String bridge in sla_std, the content of encoded forms is asserted by value in tests (Examples 2–3) rather than printed.

Example 2: Value Semantics and Slicing

@import "sla_std/bytes.sla"

@test "doc value semantics"() {
    let s = format("abc");
    let b = bytes_from_str(&s);
    let r = bytes_set(&b, 0, 65u8);
    if (bytes_get(&r, 0) as i64) != 65 { panic(1); };
    if (bytes_get(&b, 0) as i64) != 97 { panic(2); };
}

@test "doc slice reverse"() {
    let s = format("0123456789");
    let b = bytes_from_str(&s);
    let e = format("987654321");
    let eb = bytes_from_str(&e);
    let r = bytes_slice(&b, 9, 0, -1);
    if !bytes_eq(&r, &eb) { panic(3); };
}

bytes_set leaves b holding "abc" and returns "Abc"; the reversed slice of "0123456789" with bounds (9, 0, -1) is "987654321" — the stop bound is exclusive, as in CPython.

Example 3: Hex Round-Trip and the Out-of-Range Panic

@import "sla_std/bytes.sla"

@test "doc hex roundtrip"() {
    let v: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
    v.push(222u8);
    v.push(173u8);
    v.push(190u8);
    v.push(239u8);
    let b = bytes_from_vec(&v);
    let e = format("deadbeef");
    let eb = bytes_from_str(&e);
    let h = bytes_to_hex(&b);
    if !bytes_eq(&h, &eb) { panic(4); };
    let r = bytes_from_hex(&e);
    if !bytes_eq(&r, &b) { panic(5); };
}

@test should_panic "doc get out of range"() {
    let s = format("abc");
    let b = bytes_from_str(&s);
    let g = bytes_get(&b, 3);
}

Panic Codes (sla_std block)

CodeCondition
9010Index out of range (bytes_get / bytes_set)
9011bytes_from_hex: odd digit count, non-hex digit, or whitespace inside a byte pair
9012bytes_from_b64: bad character, bad padding, or bad length
9013bytes_slice: step zero
NoteThe psa runtime's dynamic bytes (tag 15, a Box<Vec<u8>> payload) is the psa side of the same settlement: the two agree on the payload shape and the carrier-pointer idiom, so psa glue can move between a tag-15 value and this Bytes type by unboxing the carrier pointer.
